name: Return on invested capital (ROIC)
seoDesc: Return on invested capital (ROIC): work out ROIC from the EBIT and the tax rate. A free finance calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: Supply the EBIT, the tax rate, the equity and the debt and the Return on invested capital (ROIC) calculator solves for ROIC. It suits a budget, a loan conversation, a payslip check or a what-if before you talk to a lender. The unit chips sit next to the boxes, which is where most hand-calculation mistakes start.

sections.title: How does the Return on invested capital (ROIC) calculator work?
sections.html:
The Return on invested capital (ROIC) calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports ROIC in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the EBIT, the tax rate, the equity and the debt.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Return on invested capital (ROIC) calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

ROIC=NOPAT ÷ invested capital
NOPAT=EBIT × (1 − tax rate)
Invested capital=debt + equity

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose NOPAT = 10 and Invested capital = 10. Working through the relationship above gives ROIC = 100 %.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: ROIC = 100 % should be roughly the size you expected from NOPAT = 10 and Invested capital = 10.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Currency, opening in US Dollar

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Return on invested capital (ROIC) calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Building a monthly budget and testing how one number shifts the rest
  • Preparing questions for a lender, an accountant or an adviser
  • Comparing two offers that quote their costs in different ways
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the EBIT, the tax rate and the equity — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Return on invested capital (ROIC) calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns ROIC, derived from the EBIT, the tax rate and the equity. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Return on invested capital (ROIC) calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the EBIT, the tax rate, the equity and the debt, which is 4 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter EBIT in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. EBIT opens in US Dollar and the chip beside it offers 113 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports ROIC = 100 %. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Return on invested capital (ROIC) calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
